items.title: NBER working paper 35275 — 'Writing Code vs. Shipping Code': Demirer, Musolff and Yang put the AI-vs-human-effort elasticity of substitution at 0.25 across 100K+ GitHub developers, read it as a human-bottleneck weak-link story
items.summary: An NBER working paper (number 35275, 'Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools' by Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, originally posted May 2026) has resurfaced this week in developer-productivity commentary as the empirical anchor for the 'code output goes up, shipped software barely moves' critique of agentic coding. The paper's matched event study tracks AI usage telemetry across more than 100,000 GitHub developers and four app marketplaces. It estimates an elasticity of substitution of 0.25 between AI and human effort, which the authors read as strong complementarity — a 'weak-link' view in which human bottlenecks (chiefly code review and release engineering) cap how much AI's task-level speedups actually reach shipped software. On the marketplace half, they find a moderate increase in new apps shipped but no corresponding increase in total marketplace usage. A widely circulated Product Hunt summary this week headlines the gap as commits up ~240% while releases are only up ~30%; the paper's own abstract wording is more cautious, and the exact headline numbers come from the summary, not from the authors, so the elasticity figure is the one worth filing. A separate LinearB 2026 benchmark, cited in secondary coverage, puts the merge rate of AI-generated pull requests at 32.7% against roughly 84.5% for human-authored code, and the queue time before review begins at 4.6x longer for AI PRs — same shape, different dataset.
items.why_it_matters: This is the clearest empirical read yet on a question every Python hobbyist starts to ask once they've used Claude Code, Cursor or an agent for a few weeks: 'OK, but is any of the extra code I'm writing actually making it into a shipped thing?' The paper's answer, at labour-economics rigor rather than vibes, is 'partially — and the limiting factor is you, not the model.' The 0.25 elasticity of substitution is the technical core: it says AI and human effort are closer to complements than substitutes in this data, which is the opposite of the 'AI replaces developers' framing most launch-day press runs with. The weak-link / human-bottleneck framing is also actionable: review speed, merge speed, test speed and the time it takes you yourself to agree the thing works are the things that most determine whether a day of agent-assisted writing turns into a release, and those are all human-side knobs. Three practical takeaways: (1) if you're using an AI coding tool and feel like you're generating a lot of code without shipping proportionally more features, the data says that is the median experience, not your personal failure — and the fix is not 'use the model more' but 'shorten your review-and-merge loop,' which for a solo hobbyist means things like better test coverage, smaller PR-sized changes, and a working CI that auto-runs on push; (2) the LinearB 32.7% vs 84.5% merge-rate gap is the number to file for anyone building agent-authored PRs into a workflow — AI-generated code is roughly 2.5x less likely to merge, so the pipeline needs to assume more rework, not less; (3) the paper's finding of 'new apps up, total usage flat' on marketplaces is the honest shape of the Cambrian-explosion debate — more things are being built, but it is not obvious yet that users are consuming more of them. The broader read: the next phase of the agentic-coding story is not another model benchmark; it is tool and workflow design that collapses the review-and-ship bottleneck. Expect vendors (GitHub, Linear, Atlassian, agentic-review startups) to pile into exactly that gap over the next two quarters.
items.why_it_matters_brief: NBER paper tracks AI's code-output boost across 100K+ GitHub developers and finds an elasticity of substitution of 0.25 with human effort — a weak-link, human-bottleneck read where review and release pace, not model speed, decide how much shipped software actually moves.

items.title: Salesforce Winter '27 goes GA today — Agentforce agents now run multi-step workflows (not just answer questions), Agentic Commerce Search self-reports a 13% conversion lift against an undisclosed baseline, Financial Services moves to production this week
items.summary: Salesforce's Winter '27 product release reached general availability on Monday, October 12, 2026 — the first release in which Agentforce, Salesforce's AI-agent layer, runs entire multi-step workflows rather than only answering questions in-context. The release packages 15 'innovations' across contact center, commerce, scheduling, Slack integration, voice, and developer tooling, and lands on top of an Agentforce auto-enablement rollout that Salesforce began the first week of September (originally planned for August, then shifted to a rolling phase-in). On commerce, Salesforce credits the new Agentic Commerce Search feature with a 13% conversion lift in early customer deployments — the number comes from Salesforce's own measurement, and the measurement window, number of merchants, and baseline are not disclosed in the public announcement, so analysts have flagged it as a vendor-reported figure rather than an independently audited one. On financial services, Agentforce Financial Services (formerly Financial Services Cloud) is moving to customers' production orgs in upgrade windows on October 2, 9, and 10 ahead of today's GA. Marketing coverage highlights two new agents for campaign creation and lead nurturing, plus email-deliverability monitoring in Marketing Cloud Next and Account Engagement. The release is the first Salesforce major-cycle where Agentforce is on by default for existing orgs rather than opt-in — a specific contractual and compliance change for customers in regulated industries that depend on explicit admin provisioning.
items.why_it_matters: Salesforce going agents-run-whole-workflows by default is the clearest 'agents are the business layer now' signal from an enterprise vendor the size of an enterprise vendor — it is the kind of release that quietly moves 'agents' from a demo category to a line item on IT budgets, because every mid-market company already paying for Salesforce now has agents running against their CRM data whether they explicitly opted in or not. For a hobbyist Python coder, the direct relevance is thin (you're not writing Apex), but the indirect read is useful in a few ways: (1) the auto-enablement model — rolling 'on by default' through existing customer orgs — is the shape the next wave of SaaS-agent rollouts will take, and it is worth watching how customers in regulated industries react, because that reaction will set the compliance template every other vendor copies; (2) the 'Agentic Commerce Search → 13% conversion lift' claim is a specific example of the AI-feature-attribution problem that is going to dominate the next year of enterprise AI reporting — a vendor can report a lift against any baseline it chooses, and 13% with no disclosed methodology is somewhere between 'real' and 'a well-selected A/B window' until an independent audit happens; it is the right skeptical lens to apply to every 'AI increased X by Y%' number from a vendor's own press release, including Salesforce's; (3) the broader framing — 'agents run the workflow, not just answer in-context' — is the industry-wide positioning shift from the chat-interface era to the business-logic-execution era, and that is also where Python-stack projects (LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex Workflows, CrewAI, Microsoft AutoGen, OpenAI's Agent SDK) are competing with the enterprise suites. The practical thing to file: when a vendor the size of Salesforce ships 'agents on by default,' the ceiling for what's acceptable in agentic release engineering just moved — Salesforce has infrastructure, compliance, and support staff for 'oops the agent did the wrong thing,' and the startups shipping similar features into a hobbyist's own workflow mostly don't. Pick agentic tools with that asymmetry in mind.
